{{Short description|Packing problem}}
[[File:Close packing box (cropped).svg|thumb|Spheres packed in a cube]]
In geometry, '''sphere packing in a cube''' is a three-dimensional [[sphere packing]] problem with the objective of packing [[sphere]]s inside a [[cube]]. It is the three-dimensional equivalent of the [[circle packing in a square]] problem in two dimensions. The problem consists of determining the optimal packing of a given number of spheres inside the cube.

Gensane<ref name=gensane>{{cite journal
 | last = Gensane | first = Th.
 | doi = 10.37236/1786
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Electronic Journal of Combinatorics
 | mr = 2056085
 | article-number = Research Paper 33
 | title = Dense packings of equal spheres in a cube
 | volume = 11
 | year = 2004| doi-access = free
 }}</ref> traces the origin of the problem to work of J. Schaer in the mid-1960s.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Schaer | first = J.
 | doi = 10.4153/CMB-1966-033-0
 | journal = Canadian Mathematical Bulletin
 | mr = 200797
 | pages = 265–270
 | title = On the densest packing of spheres in a cube
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1966
 | issue = 3
 }}</ref> Reviewing Schaer's work, [[H. S. M. Coxeter]] writes that he "proves that the arrangements for <math>k=2,3,4,8,9</math> are what anyone would have guessed".<ref>Coxeter, {{MR|200797}}</ref> The cases <math>k=7</math> and <math>k=10</math> were resolved in later work of Schaer,<ref>{{cite conference
 | last = Schaer | first = J.
 | contribution = The densest packing of ten congruent spheres in a cube
 | isbn = 0-444-81906-1
 | mr = 1383635
 | pages = 403–424
 | publisher = North-Holland | location = Amsterdam
 | series = Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai
 | title = Intuitive geometry (Szeged, 1991)
 | volume = 63
 | year = 1994}}</ref> and a packing for <math>k=14</math> was proven optimal by Joós.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Joós | first = Antal
 | doi = 10.1007/s10711-008-9308-3
 | journal = Geometriae Dedicata
 | mr = 2504734
 | pages = 49–80
 | title = On the packing of fourteen congruent spheres in a cube
 | volume = 140
 | year = 2009}}</ref> For larger numbers of spheres, all results so far are conjectural.<ref name=gensane/> In a 1971 paper, Goldberg found many non-optimal packings for other values of <math>k</math> and three that may still be optimal.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Goldberg | first = Michael
 | doi = 10.2307/2689076
 | journal = Mathematics Magazine
 | jstor = 2689076
 | mr = 298562
 | pages = 199–208
 | title = On the densest packing of equal spheres in a cube
 | volume = 44
 | year = 1971
 | issue = 4
 }}</ref> Gensane improved the rest of Goldberg's packings and found good packings for up to 32 spheres.<ref name=gensane/>

Goldberg also conjectured that for numbers of spheres of the form <math>k=\lceil p^3/2\rceil</math>, the optimal packing of spheres in a cube is a form of [[Close-packing of equal spheres|cubic close-packing]]. However, omitting as few as two spheres from this number allows a different and tighter packing.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Tatarevic | first = Milos
 | doi = 10.37236/3784
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Electronic Journal of Combinatorics
 | mr = 3315477
 | article-number = Paper 1.35
 | title = On limits of dense packing of equal spheres in a cube
 | volume = 22
 | year = 2015| arxiv = 1503.07933
 }}</ref>
